chapter.name: Wave Optics
chapter.blurb: The chapter treats light as a wave. It uses Huygens principle and wavefronts to derive the laws of reflection and refraction, then explains interference through the coherent addition of waves and Young's double-slit experiment. It ends with diffraction at a single slit and the polarisation of light by polaroids, including Malus' law.

scope_in.item: Recall how the wave model of light came to be accepted (corpuscular versus wave prediction for the speed of light in a denser medium, Young's interference experiment, Maxwell's electromagnetic theory explaining propagation in vacuum) and define geometrical optics and a ray as the limit of wavelength tending to zero

Define a wavefront as a surface of constant phase, state that energy travels perpendicular to it, and identify spherical and plane wavefronts for a point source, a distant source and light leaving a convex lens with a point source at its focus
State Huygens principle and use the construction (secondary wavelets of radius vt, forward envelope) to find a later wavefront; explain the backwave and Huygens' ad hoc assumption
Derive sin i / sin r = v1/v2 and Snell's law n1 sin i = n2 sin r from Huygens' construction, and use n = c/v
Use lambda1/lambda2 = v1/v2 with unchanged frequency to find speed, wavelength and frequency of refracted light; state that a wave bending towards the normal is slower in the second medium
Describe refraction at a rarer medium with Huygens' construction, define the critical angle by sin ic = n2/n1 and explain total internal reflection for i greater than ic
Derive the law of reflection from Huygens' construction using congruent triangles

Describe how a plane wavefront is changed by a thin prism, a convex lens and a concave mirror (and by analogy a concave lens and convex mirror), and state that the time of travel from object point to image point is the same along any ray

Explain why reflected and refracted light keep the incident frequency, that a fall in speed does not imply a fall in energy, and what determines intensity in the wave and photon pictures (Example 10.1)
State the superposition principle, define coherent and incoherent sources, and apply the path-difference conditions n lambda (constructive, 4 I0) and (n + 1/2) lambda (destructive, zero)
Convert path difference to phase difference, derive and use I = 4 I0 cos^2(phi/2) for two equal coherent waves, and use I = 2 I0 for incoherent sources
Explain why two independent sources give no fringes and how Young's arrangement locks the phases of the two pinholes

Use the path difference xd/D, the bright-fringe positions x = n lambda D/d and dark-fringe positions x = (n + 1/2) lambda D/d, and the equal fringe spacing lambda D/d in Young's double-slit experiment, including coincidence of fringes of two wavelengths

Describe diffraction as a general wave phenomenon and the single-slit pattern: central maximum at theta = 0, minima at theta = n lambda/a, weaker secondary maxima at theta = (n + 1/2) lambda/a; work out the angular extent of the central maximum from the first minima

State Feynman's remark on interference versus diffraction, that the double-slit pattern is a superposition of single-slit diffraction and double-slit interference, how to see the single-slit pattern with two razor blades and a bulb filament, and that energy is only redistributed in interference and diffraction

Describe linearly (plane) polarised and unpolarised transverse waves, that light is transverse, and how a polaroid with aligned long-chain molecules and a pass-axis linearly polarises light and halves the intensity of unpolarised light
Apply Malus' law I = I0 cos^2(theta) to two polaroids and to a polaroid between two crossed polaroids, I = (I0/4) sin^2(2 theta); list uses of polaroids

concepts.name: The wave model of light, wavefronts and Huygens principle
concepts.description: How the wave theory of light came to be accepted, what a wavefront and a ray are, spherical and plane wavefronts, and Huygens' geometrical construction for finding a later wavefront.
concepts.idea: Light is a wave; a wavefront is a surface of constant phase, and every point on it acts as a source of secondary wavelets whose forward envelope is the wavefront a moment later.
concepts.rule: A wavefront is a locus of points that oscillate in phase, i.e. a surface of constant phase. The speed with which the wavefront moves outwards from the source is the speed of the wave, and the energy of the wave travels perpendicular to the wavefront. A point source emitting uniformly gives spherical wavefronts; at a large distance from the source a small portion of the sphere is a plane wavefront. Huygens principle: each point of a wavefront is a source of secondary wavelets that spread out in all directions with the speed of the wave; after time t each wavelet is a sphere of radius vt, and the common tangent (forward envelope) to these spheres is the new wavefront. The construction also gives a backwave, which does not exist; Huygens assumed, ad hoc, that the wavelet amplitude is maximum in the forward direction and zero in the backward direction, and the absence of the backwave is really justified by more rigorous wave theory. Geometrical optics is the branch of optics that completely neglects the finiteness of the wavelength; a ray is the path of energy propagation in the limit of wavelength tending to zero. The wave theory was slow to be accepted because of Newton's authority and because light travels through vacuum; Young's interference experiment established the wave nature and Maxwell's electromagnetic theory explained propagation in vacuum.
concepts.example: A spherical wavefront of radius 1.0 m around a point source in air becomes, 1.0 ns later, a spherical wavefront of radius 1.0 m + (3 x 10^8 m/s)(1.0 x 10^-9 s) = 1.3 m.

questions.q: In the nineteenth century the main difficulty with the wave theory of light was that light reaches us through vacuum. Explain how Maxwell's work removed this difficulty.
questions.a: It was believed that a wave always needs a medium. Maxwell showed from his equations of electricity and magnetism that electromagnetic waves exist, with a speed in free space very close to the measured speed of light, so light is an electromagnetic wave. A changing electric field produces a changing magnetic field and vice versa, and these changing fields propagate even in vacuum, so no material medium is needed.
s: Light is an electromagnetic wave (predicted speed of such waves matches the speed of light)
Changing electric and magnetic fields produce each other and propagate even in vacuum, so no medium is required

questions.a: (a) Radius of each wavelet = vt = (3.0 x 10^8 m/s)(0.50 x 10^-9 s) = 0.15 m. (c) The wavelets also have a backward envelope, a sphere of radius 0.30 m - 0.15 m = 0.15 m (the backwave). It does not exist: there is no wave travelling back towards the source.
s: Wavelet radius vt = 0.15 m
New wavefront is a sphere centred on O of radius 0.45 m (forward envelope)
Backward envelope of radius 0.15 m is the backwave, which does not exist

questions.q: Rays are lines drawn perpendicular to the wavefronts. Use this to describe the rays for (a) the spherical wavefronts spreading from a point source and (b) a plane wavefront, giving the reason rays are drawn this way.
questions.a: The energy of a wave travels perpendicular to the wavefront, so rays are drawn normal to the wavefronts. s: Reason - energy travels perpendicular to the wavefront, so rays are normals to it

questions.q: Huygens' construction applied to a diverging spherical wavefront gives two envelopes of the secondary wavelets, one ahead of the wavefront and one behind it. Explain which of the two is the actual wavefront, how Huygens accounted for the other, and why his account is regarded as unsatisfactory.
questions.a: The envelope ahead of the wavefront (the forward envelope) is the actual new wavefront. The envelope behind it would be a backwave travelling towards the source, and no such wave exists. Huygens accounted for this by assuming that the amplitude of the secondary wavelets is maximum in the forward direction and zero in the backward direction. This is an ad hoc assumption made only to remove the backwave; it is not satisfactory, and the absence of the backwave is really justified only from more rigorous wave theory.
s: The forward envelope is the real wavefront; the backward envelope (backwave) does not exist
Huygens assumed wavelet amplitude is maximum forward and zero backward
This is an ad hoc assumption; the real justification comes from more rigorous wave theory

questions.q: A student says: 'Huygens' wave theory was not accepted at first because it could not explain the reflection and refraction of light.' Evaluate this statement.
questions.a: The statement is wrong. The wave model explained reflection and refraction satisfactorily. It was not readily accepted mainly because of Newton's authority behind the corpuscular model, and because light travels through vacuum whereas it was felt that a wave always needs a medium.
s: Judgement - wrong: the wave theory did explain reflection and refraction
Actual reasons - Newton's authority, and the belief that a wave needs a medium while light crosses vacuum

questions.q: Devise a simple demonstration with a calm pool of water that shows what a wavefront is, and explain how the same demonstration shows the speed of the wave and the direction in which its energy travels.
questions.a: Drop a small stone into a calm pool. Waves spread out from the point of impact and, at any instant, circular rings of maximum disturbance are seen. All points on one ring are at the same distance from the point of impact, so they oscillate in phase: each ring is a wavefront (a locus of constant phase). The rings grow steadily; the speed with which a ring moves outwards from the source is the speed of the wave. The rings move radially outwards, at right angles to themselves, showing that the energy travels perpendicular to the wavefront.
s: Set-up - stone dropped in a calm pool gives circular rings spreading from the point of impact
Each ring is a wavefront because all its points are equidistant from the source and oscillate in phase
Outward speed of a ring is the wave speed, and the motion is perpendicular to the ring (direction of energy flow)

concepts.name: Refraction of a plane wave by Huygens principle
concepts.description: Derivation of Snell's law from Huygens' construction, the change of speed and wavelength with unchanged frequency, refraction at a rarer medium and the critical angle.
concepts.idea: A wavefront swings round on entering a second medium because its wavelets travel at a different speed there, and this fixes the ratio of the sines of the two angles.
concepts.rule: For a plane wavefront AB incident at angle i on the surface between medium 1 (speed v1) and medium 2 (speed v2): in the time t that B takes to reach the surface at C, BC = v1 t, and the wavelet from A is a sphere of radius AE = v2 t in medium 2; the tangent plane CE is the refracted wavefront. From triangles ABC and AEC, sin i = BC/AC and sin r = AE/AC, so sin i / sin r = v1/v2. With n1 = c/v1 and n2 = c/v2 this is Snell's law n1 sin i = n2 sin r. If r < i (bending towards the normal) then v2 < v1, the prediction of the wave theory. The wavelengths satisfy lambda1/lambda2 = v1/v2, i.e. v1/lambda1 = v2/lambda2: on entering a denser medium the speed and the wavelength decrease but the frequency (v/lambda) stays the same. For refraction at a rarer medium (v2 > v1) the wave bends away from the normal, r > i; the critical angle is given by sin ic = n2/n1, at which r = 90 degrees, and for i > ic there is no refracted wave and the wave is totally internally reflected. The energy carried by a wave depends on its amplitude, not on its speed.
concepts.example: Light of wavelength 660 nm in air enters glass of refractive index 1.5: its wavelength there is 660/1.5 = 440 nm, while its frequency is unchanged.

For i > ic, sin r would exceed 1, which is impossible, so there is no refracted wave (total internal reflection)

Draw the tangent plane CE from C to this sphere; CE is the refracted wavefront and makes angle r with the surface. Since sin i = BC/AC and sin r = AE/AC with AE > BC, sin r > sin i, so r > i: the refracted wavefront is tilted more steeply to the surface and the wave bends away from the normal.
s: BC = v1 t marked, and a wavelet of radius AE = v2 t (larger than BC) drawn from A in the rarer medium
Tangent plane CE from C drawn as the refracted wavefront
sin r / sin i = AE/BC = v2/v1 > 1, so r > i and the wave bends away from the normal

concepts.name: Reflection of a plane wave and the behaviour of wavefronts at prisms, lenses and mirrors
concepts.description: The law of reflection from Huygens' construction, how a plane wavefront is changed by a thin prism, a convex lens and a concave mirror, equality of travel time along all rays, and why frequency is unchanged on reflection and refraction.
concepts.idea: Parts of a wavefront that spend longer in glass, or that are reflected later, fall behind, and this delay reshapes the wavefront.
concepts.rule: Reflection: a plane wavefront AB is incident at angle i on a reflecting surface MN; in the time t that B takes to reach the surface at C (BC = vt) the wavelet from A is a sphere of radius AE = vt, and the tangent plane CE is the reflected wavefront. Triangles EAC and BAC are congruent, so the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. Thin prism: the part of a plane wavefront that passes through the greatest thickness of glass is delayed most (light is slower in glass), so the emerging wavefront is plane but tilted. Convex lens: the central part of the wavefront crosses the thickest glass and is delayed most, so the emerging wavefront is spherical and converges to the focus F. Concave mirror: a plane wave is reflected as a spherical wave converging to the focus F. The total time from a point on the object to the corresponding point on the image is the same along every ray. Reflected and refracted light have the same frequency as the incident light, because the atoms of the medium act as oscillators forced at the frequency of the incident light. In the wave picture intensity is determined by the square of the amplitude; in the photon picture, for a given frequency, by the number of photons crossing unit area per unit time.
concepts.example: A plane wavefront inclined at 20 degrees to a plane mirror is reflected as a plane wavefront inclined at 20 degrees to the mirror on the other side of the normal.

s: Central part of the plane wavefront reaches the bulging centre of the mirror and is reflected first
Outer parts are reflected later, so they lag behind the centre
Reflected wavefront is spherical and diverging, as if from a point behind the mirror

concepts.name: Coherent and incoherent addition of waves
concepts.description: The superposition principle, coherent sources, conditions on path and phase difference for constructive and destructive interference, the resultant intensity for a given phase difference, and the addition of intensities for incoherent sources.
concepts.idea: Displacements add, not intensities: two coherent waves can reinforce to four times one intensity or cancel to zero, but incoherent waves just add their intensities.
concepts.rule: Superposition principle: the resultant displacement at a point is the vector sum of the displacements produced by each wave. Two sources are coherent if the phase difference between the displacements they produce at a point does not change with time. For two coherent sources S1 and S2 vibrating in phase, each giving intensity I0 alone: a path difference S1P ~ S2P = n lambda (n = 0, 1, 2, ...) gives constructive interference with resultant intensity 4 I0; a path difference (n + 1/2) lambda gives destructive interference with zero intensity. A path difference of lambda corresponds to a phase difference of 2 pi. For a phase difference phi, y1 = a cos(omega t) and y2 = a cos(omega t + phi) add to an amplitude 2a cos(phi/2), so I = 4 I0 cos^2(phi/2). The distances to the point are taken to be much greater than the source separation d so that the two amplitudes are nearly equal. If the phase difference between the sources changes rapidly with time the sources are incoherent, the pattern is washed out and the time-averaged intensity is I = 2 I0 at all points: the intensities just add, as when two separate light sources illuminate a wall.
concepts.example: Two coherent sources vibrating in phase, each giving intensity I0 alone, produce 4 I0 at a point where the path difference is 2 lambda (phase difference 4 pi) and 2 I0 where it is 1.25 lambda (phase difference 2.5 pi, since cos^2(1.25 pi) = 1/2).

Observed intensity is 2 I0 at all points (intensities add)

questions.a: Zero path difference gives the maximum, 4 I0 = 80 units. A path difference of lambda/3 corresponds to a phase difference phi = (2 pi/lambda)(lambda/3) = 2 pi/3. I = 4 I0 cos^2(phi/2) = 80 x cos^2(60 degrees) = 80 x 0.25 = 20 units.

I = 4 I0 cos^2(phi/2) = 80 x 0.25 = 20 units

At Q: path difference = 1200/400 = 3 lambda; phase difference = 6 pi. This is of the form n lambda, so the interference is constructive and I = 4 I0 = 4 x 2 = 8 mW/m^2.
s: P: 3.5 lambda, phase difference 7 pi; Q: 3 lambda, phase difference 6 pi
P is destructive: intensity zero

questions.a: It is assumed that the distances S1Q and S2Q are much greater than the separation d of the sources, so that although the two distances are not equal, the amplitudes of the displacements produced by the two waves at Q are very nearly the same. Equal amplitudes are needed for the two displacements to cancel completely when they are out of phase, giving exactly zero intensity.
s: Assumption - S1Q and S2Q are much greater than d, so the two amplitudes are very nearly equal
Only equal amplitudes cancel completely to give zero intensity at destructive interference

Derive the resultant intensity at G in terms of I0 and phi, and deduce the values of phi for maximum and for zero intensity. You may use cos A + cos B = 2 cos((A + B)/2) cos((A - B)/2).
questions.a: y = y1 + y2 = a[cos(omega t) + cos(omega t + phi)] = 2a cos(phi/2) cos(omega t + phi/2). The amplitude of the resultant displacement is 2a cos(phi/2). Intensity is proportional to the square of the amplitude, and I0 is proportional to a^2, so I = 4 I0 cos^2(phi/2). The intensity is maximum (4 I0) when phi = 0, +/- 2 pi, +/- 4 pi, ... and zero when phi = +/- pi, +/- 3 pi, +/- 5 pi, ...
s: Resultant y = 2a cos(phi/2) cos(omega t + phi/2), amplitude 2a cos(phi/2)
I = 4 I0 cos^2(phi/2), since intensity is proportional to amplitude squared
Maximum for phi = 0, +/- 2 pi, +/- 4 pi ...; zero for phi = +/- pi, +/- 3 pi ...

questions.q: A student claims: 'Two coherent sources give an intensity of 4 I0, while two incoherent sources give only 2 I0, so making sources coherent doubles the total light energy.' Evaluate this claim.

Coherence only redistributes the energy between bright and dark regions; it does not create energy.
s: Judgement - wrong: 4 I0 occurs only at maxima, with zero at minima
Average over the pattern is 2 I0, as for incoherent sources - energy is only redistributed

questions.q: Design a demonstration with a trough of water and two needles to show (a) a stable interference pattern from coherent sources and (b) what happens when the sources are not coherent. Say what is seen in each case.
questions.a: (a) Make the two needles S1 and S2 move up and down periodically in an identical fashion, for example by fixing both to the same vibrating arm so that they stay in step. A stable pattern is seen on the water: lines of maximum displacement (antinodal lines, where the path difference is a whole number of wavelengths) alternating with lines of no displacement (nodal lines, where it is an odd number of half wavelengths). (b) Now drive the two needles separately so that their phase difference keeps changing rapidly. The positions of the maxima and minima shift rapidly, no fixed nodal and antinodal lines are seen, and the disturbance appears uniform on average.
s: Two needles driven in an identical fashion (in step) act as coherent sources
Stable pattern of antinodal (maximum) and nodal (no displacement) lines is seen
With an unsteady phase difference the pattern shifts rapidly and averages out to a uniform disturbance

concepts.name: Interference of light and Young's double-slit experiment
concepts.description: Why independent light sources do not give fringes, how Young obtained two coherent sources, and the positions and spacing of the bright and dark fringes.
concepts.idea: Two pinholes lit from one source are locked in phase, so their light gives a steady pattern of equally spaced bright and dark fringes.
concepts.rule: Light from an ordinary source such as a sodium lamp undergoes abrupt phase changes in times of the order of 10^-10 s, so two independent sources have no fixed phase relationship, are incoherent, and their intensities simply add: no fringes. Young illuminated two closely spaced pinholes S1 and S2 from a single pinhole S lit by a bright source; any abrupt phase change in S appears identically in S1 and S2, so they are locked in phase (coherent). For slit separation d and screen distance D, the path difference at a point a distance x from the centre of the screen is xd/D. Bright fringes: xd/D = n lambda, x_n = n lambda D/d, n = 0, +/-1, +/-2, ... (n = 0 is the central bright fringe). Dark fringes: xd/D = (n + 1/2) lambda, x_n = (n + 1/2) lambda D/d. Dark and bright fringes are equally spaced; the spacing between adjacent bright (or adjacent dark) fringes is lambda D/d.
concepts.example: With d = 0.025 mm, D = 5 cm and lambda = 500 nm the fringe spacing is lambda D/d = (5 x 10^-7 m)(0.05 m)/(2.5 x 10^-5 m) = 1 x 10^-3 m = 1 mm.

questions.q: You are given a source of light of wavelength 600 nm and a screen that must stand 1.5 m from a pair of slits. concepts.name: Diffraction at a single slit
concepts.description: Diffraction as a general wave phenomenon, the single-slit pattern with its central maximum, the angular positions of minima and secondary maxima, how to see the pattern, and the redistribution of energy.
concepts.idea: Light spreads out on passing through a narrow slit, giving a broad central bright band flanked by weaker bands, and the narrower the slit the more it spreads.
concepts.rule: Diffraction is a general characteristic of all types of waves (sound, light, water, matter waves). Because the wavelength of light is much smaller than the dimensions of most obstacles, diffraction of light is not met in everyday observation. For a parallel beam of wavelength lambda falling normally on a single slit of width a, the different parts of the wavefront at the slit act as secondary sources in phase; their contributions at a point in direction theta are added with the proper phase differences. The pattern has a central maximum at theta = 0; minima (zero intensity) at theta approximately n lambda/a, n = +/-1, +/-2, +/-3, ...; and secondary maxima at theta approximately (n + 1/2) lambda/a, which become weaker with increasing n (theta in radian). The central maximum therefore extends from -lambda/a to +lambda/a. The pattern in a double-slit experiment is a superposition of single-slit diffraction from each slit and the double-slit interference pattern; according to Feynman there is no specific, important physical difference between interference and diffraction, the usage depending on whether few or many sources are involved. The single-slit pattern can be seen by viewing a straight bulb filament through the narrow gap between two razor blades held parallel to it; fringes are wider for red than for blue. In interference and diffraction light energy is redistributed, with no gain or loss of energy.
concepts.example: For a slit of width 0.5 mm and light of wavelength 500 nm the first minimum is at theta = lambda/a = (5 x 10^-7 m)/(5 x 10^-4 m) = 1 x 10^-3 rad.

Precaution - never use direct sunlight (harms the eye and gives no fringes)

concepts.name: Polarisation, polaroids and Malus' law
concepts.description: Linearly polarised and unpolarised transverse waves, the action of a polaroid and its pass-axis, the halving of unpolarised light by one polaroid, Malus' law for two polaroids, and a polaroid placed between crossed polaroids.
concepts.idea: Light is a transverse wave, so a polaroid can pick out one direction of its electric vector, and a second polaroid then passes a fraction cos^2(theta) of that light.
concepts.rule: A wave on a string whose displacement stays along one line (say y) at right angles to the direction of propagation is a transverse wave that is linearly polarised (plane polarised, here y-polarised). If the plane of vibration changes randomly in very short intervals of time the wave is unpolarised. Light waves are transverse: the electric field is always at right angles to the direction of propagation. A polaroid consists of long chain molecules aligned in one direction; electric vectors along the aligned molecules are absorbed, so the transmitted light is linearly polarised with its electric vector along the pass-axis, which is perpendicular to the aligned molecules. Unpolarised light passing through one polaroid has its intensity reduced by half, and rotating that polaroid has no effect on the transmitted intensity. If polarised light of intensity I0 falls on a second polaroid whose pass-axis makes an angle theta with that of the first, the component E cos(theta) passes and I = I0 cos^2(theta) (Malus' law): maximum at theta = 0 and nearly zero for crossed polaroids (theta = 90 degrees). With two polaroids the intensity can be controlled from 50% to zero of the incident unpolarised intensity. For a polaroid placed between two crossed polaroids at angle theta to the first, I = I0 cos^2(theta) sin^2(theta) = (I0/4) sin^2(2 theta), maximum at theta = 45 degrees. Polaroids are used in sunglasses, windowpanes, photographic cameras and 3D movie cameras.
concepts.example: Unpolarised light of intensity 100 units becomes 50 units after one polaroid; a second polaroid with its pass-axis at 60 degrees to the first passes 50 x cos^2(60 degrees) = 12.5 units.

questions.a: When one polaroid is rotated, the intensity transmitted by the pair changes from a maximum to nearly zero when the pass-axes are crossed. If the vibration were along the direction of propagation, rotating a polaroid about the beam would make no difference.

Since P1 and P3 are crossed, the angle between the pass-axes of P2 and P3 is (90 degrees - theta), so the intensity after P3 is I = I0 cos^2(theta) cos^2(90 degrees - theta) = I0 cos^2(theta) sin^2(theta) = (I0/4) sin^2(2 theta). This is maximum when sin(2 theta) = 1, i.e. theta = 45 degrees (pi/4), where I = I0/4.
s: Intensity after P2 = I0 cos^2(theta)
Angle between P2 and P3 is 90 degrees - theta, giving I = I0 cos^2(theta) sin^2(theta) = (I0/4) sin^2(2 theta)
Maximum at theta = 45 degrees

questions.q: A student claims: 'With two polaroids I can adjust the brightness of an unpolarised beam to anything from 100% down to 0% of its original intensity just by turning one of them.' Evaluate this claim.
questions.a: The claim is only partly right. The first polaroid always halves the intensity of the unpolarised beam, whatever its orientation, so at most 50% can emerge. Turning the second polaroid then varies the output as cos^2(theta), from 50% (pass-axes parallel) down to zero (pass-axes crossed). The range is 50% to 0%, not 100% to 0%.
s: First polaroid transmits only half the unpolarised intensity at any orientation
So the controllable range is from 50% to zero of the incident intensity, not from 100%

questions.a: Fix one polaroid sheet in the window frame and mount a second sheet over it so that it can be rotated in its own plane. Unpolarised daylight is linearly polarised by the first sheet (with half its intensity transmitted); the second sheet then transmits I = I0 cos^2(theta), where I0 is the intensity after the first sheet and theta is the angle between the two pass-axes (Malus' law). Brightest view: theta = 0 (pass-axes parallel), I = I0. Half of the brightest: cos^2(theta) = 1/2, i.e. theta = 45 degrees. Dark window: theta = 90 degrees (crossed), I nearly zero.
s: Arrangement - one fixed polaroid and a second one that can be rotated over it
Law - I = I0 cos^2(theta), theta being the angle between the pass-axes
Settings - 0 degrees brightest, 45 degrees half, 90 degrees dark
